source.author_body: I've been building Zaivy, a platform designed to help people figure out which business or side hustle fits their situation and what to do next. One of the biggest problems I ran into was that recommendations could sound personalized without actually explaining much. Someone might receive five opportunities with high fit percentages, but that doesn't necessarily mean they understand why those opportunities were recommended. So I've spent the past few weeks improving that. Zaivy can now collect activity-specific experience, compare it against reviewed opportunity requirements, and explain why someone's reported experience may be relevant to a particular opportunity. I've also worked on making the explanations more transparent about missing information and what the system can't confidently determine. The automated tests are passing, but I know that doesn't prove the recommendations are actually useful. That's what I want to figure out next. I'm preparing a small usability round with five people to answer three questions: Do people understand why an opportunity was recommended? Does the recommendation actually reflect their situation? Can they identify a realistic next step after using Zaivy? I'm also questioning whether displaying precise fit percentages is the right approach when the underlying model hasn't been validated against real-world outcomes. My question for other founders: When you're building a product that makes personalized recommendations, how do you determine whether users genuinely trust the reasoning instead of just trusting the numbers? Also, if anyone is interested in trying Zaivy and giving critical feedback, I'd appreciate it. I'm specifically looking for people who are unsure what kind of business or side hustle they want to pursue.

metadata.headline: I spent weeks improving my startup's recommendations. Now I need to find out if they're actually useful.

source.decision: Discussion/seller/product research only; no paid buyer or complete competition/contact evidence
